slides.narration: Radio, Wi-Fi, sunlight and hospital X-rays all have something in common: they are waves of electric and magnetic field that need no medium at all. In this part we meet the idea that made them possible, the displacement current in a charging capacitor, then see how changing fields keep each other going as a transverse wave, and work out its speed from two constants of empty space.

slides.heading: Ampère’s law meets a charging capacitor
slides.body_md: Ampère’s circuital law, $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 i$, uses the current through **any** surface bounded by the loop. Take a loop round the lead of a capacitor that is being charged:
bullets: A flat disc spanning the loop is crossed by the wire: enclosed current $i$.
A bag-shaped surface on the same loop, bulging through the **gap**, is crossed by no charge: enclosed current **zero**.
Same loop, two answers: the law as it stood is incomplete.

slides.narration: Ampère’s law says the magnetic field round a loop depends on the current through any surface the loop bounds. Draw a loop round the wire leading to a charging capacitor. A flat disc on that loop is pierced by the wire, so the enclosed current is i. But a bag on the same loop can pass through the gap, where no charge flows, giving zero. One loop cannot have two fields, so something is missing.

slides.heading: Displacement current
slides.body_md:
Maxwell noticed that in the gap the **electric flux is changing**. He added a **displacement current**
$$i_d = \varepsilon_0\,\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$$
For parallel plates, $\Phi_E = EA = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $i_d = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = i$: the current is **continuous** through the gap.
bullets: Ampère–Maxwell law: $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0(i + i_d)$.
Basic idea only in ISC: use $i_d = \varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt$ as a formula.

slides.narration: In the gap, nothing flows, but the electric field is growing as charge piles up on the plates. Maxwell treated this changing electric flux as a current of its own, the displacement current, epsilon nought times the rate of change of electric flux. Between parallel plates the flux is the charge divided by epsilon nought, so the displacement current equals the rate of arrival of charge: exactly the current in the wires. The current is continuous after all.

slides.heading: A changing electric field makes a magnetic field
slides.body_md: The displacement current produces a magnetic field just as a conduction current does: field lines are **circles** round the axis of the plates, inside the gap and beyond its edge.
bullets: Its direction follows the right-hand rule, as for a wire carrying the current $i_d$.
It exists only while $E$ is changing: once the capacitor is fully charged, $i_d = 0$ and this field vanishes.

Measurements show a magnetic field in the gap, its lines forming circles round the axis, clockwise here, just as round a wire carrying the same current. slides.heading: Worked example 1: displacement current from a changing field
slides.body_md: A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 0.040 m² and a gap of 1.5 mm. The p.d. across it is rising at $6.0 \times 10^{5}$ V s⁻¹. Find the displacement current, and check it against the charging current.
bullets: Step 1 — $\dfrac{dE}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{d}\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{5}}{1.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.0 \times 10^{8}$ V m⁻¹ s⁻¹, so $\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = A\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 1.6 \times 10^{7}$ V m s⁻¹.
Step 2 — $i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 1.6 \times 10^{7} = 1.42 \times 10^{-4}$ A (about 0.14 mA).
Check — $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d} = 2.36 \times 10^{-10}$ F and $i = C\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 1.42 \times 10^{-4}$ A: the same.

rows: Rate of change of electric flux

visual.alt: Worked table: the field grows at four times ten to the eight volts per metre per second, the flux at one point six times ten to the seven, and the displacement current and the charging current are both 0.142 milliamperes

slides.narration: The field in the gap is the voltage over the gap, so it grows at four times ten to the eight volts per metre every second. Multiply by the plate area for the rate of change of flux, then by epsilon nought: the displacement current is about point one four milliamperes. Working out the capacitance and multiplying by the rate of rise of voltage gives the very same current in the leads, as it must.

slides.heading: Reading a charge–time graph
slides.body_md: Since $i_d = dq/dt$ for a parallel-plate capacitor, the displacement current is the **slope** of the $q$–$t$ graph:
bullets: 0 to 2 ms: slope 3.0 μC per ms, so $i_d$ = 3.0 mA.
2 ms to 4 ms: charge steady, so $i_d$ = 0, however much charge is stored.
4 ms to 5 ms: slope −6.0 μC per ms, so 6.0 mA in the **opposite** direction (discharging).

y.label: charge on the positive plate q (μC)

visual.alt: Charge on a capacitor plate against time: it rises steadily to 6 microcoulombs in 2 milliseconds, stays level for 2 milliseconds, then falls to zero in 1 millisecond
visual.caption: The displacement current in the gap is the slope: 3.0 mA, then zero, then 6.0 mA in the opposite sense.

slides.narration: Because the displacement current equals the rate of change of charge, we can read it from a graph of charge against time. While the charge climbs steadily, the displacement current is three milliamperes. While the charge stays put, it is zero, even though the plates are fully charged. When the capacitor discharges in one millisecond, the slope is twice as steep and negative: six milliamperes, the other way.

slides.heading: Conduction and displacement current compared
slides.body_md: Both kinds of current produce magnetic fields; only one involves moving charges.
bullets: In a circuit with a capacitor, the two together make a **continuous** current all the way round.

rows: Anywhere E changes: a capacitor gap, even vacuum
Yes, exactly like a conduction current

slides.heading: How an EM wave keeps itself going
slides.body_md: Faraday: a **changing B** produces an E field. Maxwell: a **changing E** produces a B field. Each regenerates the other, so the disturbance can travel through empty space.
bullets: Source: an **accelerated** charge, such as electrons oscillating in an aerial at frequency f, which radiate waves of the same frequency.
A charge at rest or moving at constant velocity does not radiate.

visual.alt: Flow of how an electromagnetic wave sustains itself: an oscillating charge makes a changing electric field, which makes a changing magnetic field, which in turn makes a changing electric field, and the linked pattern travels outward at the speed of light

slides.narration: Now put the two laws side by side. Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Maxwell added that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field. So once something starts the fields changing, each keeps regenerating the other, and the pattern moves outwards. That something is an accelerated charge, for example electrons rushing up and down an aerial, which radiate waves of their own frequency.

slides.heading: The transverse nature of EM waves
slides.body_md:
In a plane EM wave travelling along $x$, $\vec E$ oscillates along $y$ and $\vec B$ along $z$:
$$\vec E \perp \vec B,\qquad \text{both} \perp \text{direction of travel}$$
bullets: The direction of travel is the direction of $\vec E \times \vec B$.
$E$ and $B$ rise and fall **in phase**, with $E_0 = cB_0$.
Qualitative only in ISC: no wave equation is needed.

slides.heading: The speed of EM waves
slides.body_md:
Maxwell’s equations predict a wave speed in vacuum
$$c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$$
and a fixed ratio of the peak fields: $\dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = c$.
bullets: The value matched the measured speed of light, so Maxwell concluded that **light is an electromagnetic wave**.
Hertz later generated and detected radio waves in the laboratory and confirmed the prediction.
For any EM wave in vacuum: $c = f\lambda$.

rows: $3.00 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹, the measured speed of light

visual.alt: Table of the two constants of free space and the speed they predict: three times ten to the eight metres per second, the speed of light

slides.narration: From his equations Maxwell found that the waves should travel at one over the square root of mu nought times epsilon nought. Put in the two constants, measured with coils and capacitors, and out comes three times ten to the eight metres per second, the speed of light. Maxwell concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. The peak electric field is always c times the peak magnetic field.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: c from two constants, and B₀ from E₀
slides.body_md: (a) Using $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹ and $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ C² N⁻¹ m⁻², evaluate $1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$. (b) An EM wave in vacuum has a peak electric field of 72 V m⁻¹. Find its peak magnetic field.
bullets: (a) $\mu_0\varepsilon_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} = 1.11 \times 10^{-17}$ s² m⁻², so $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Worked table: mu nought epsilon nought is 1.11 times ten to the minus seventeen, giving c of three times ten to the eight metres per second; a 72 volt per metre wave has a peak magnetic field of 0.24 microtesla

slides.narration: Multiply the two constants: about one point one one times ten to the minus seventeen. The square root of that is about three point three times ten to the minus nine, and one over it is three point zero zero times ten to the eight metres per second. For part b, divide the peak electric field, seventy two volts per metre, by the speed of light: the peak magnetic field is only point two four microtesla.

slides.heading: Properties common to all EM waves
slides.body_md: Whatever their frequency, all electromagnetic waves share these properties:
bullets: They differ only in frequency (and so wavelength), which decides how they are produced, detected and used.

rows: E and B are at right angles to the direction of travel
Same for radio waves and gamma rays
They cross empty space from the Sun and stars
E and B in phase, E₀ = cB₀
They warm, push and can be absorbed
Not deflected by E or B fields
Reflect, refract, interfere, diffract and can be polarised

slides.narration: From long radio waves to the shortest gamma rays, every electromagnetic wave is transverse, travels at the same speed c in vacuum, and needs no medium. Its fields are in phase. It carries energy and momentum, it is not bent by electric or magnetic fields because it has no charge, and it obeys c equals f lambda. The only thing that changes from band to band is the frequency.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a Wi-Fi wave
slides.body_md: A Wi-Fi router transmits at 2.4 GHz. Find (a) the wavelength, (b) the period of the oscillating fields, (c) the time the wave takes to cross a 30 m house, and how many wavelengths fit in that distance.

visual.alt: Worked table: wavelength 12.5 centimetres, period 4.17 times ten to the minus ten seconds, a tenth of a microsecond to cross 30 metres, which holds 240 wavelengths

slides.narration: Divide the speed of light by two point four gigahertz: the wavelength is twelve and a half centimetres. The fields complete one oscillation in about four tenths of a nanosecond. Crossing a thirty metre house takes a tenth of a microsecond, and two hundred and forty wavelengths fit into that distance.

slides.narration: To sum up: a changing electric flux acts as a displacement current, epsilon nought d phi E by d t, which equals the charging current and keeps the current continuous through a capacitor. Accelerated charges radiate electromagnetic waves, in which E and B are at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. In vacuum they travel at one over root mu nought epsilon nought, the speed of light, with E nought equal to c times B nought.

slides.narration: A radio mast, a microwave oven, a TV remote, your eyes, a germ-killing lamp, an X-ray machine and a cancer-therapy unit all deal with the same kind of wave. Only the frequency is different. In this part we arrange the bands in order, learn their rough ranges, and for each one see how it is produced, how it is detected and what it is used for.

slides.heading: Seven bands and their ranges
slides.body_md: In order of **increasing frequency** (decreasing wavelength): radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
bullets: The boundaries are approximate; neighbouring bands overlap.
X-rays and gamma rays of the same wavelength are identical; they are named by their **origin** (electrons for X-rays, nuclei for gamma rays).

visual.alt: Table of approximate wavelength and frequency ranges of the seven bands, from radio waves longer than 30 centimetres to gamma rays shorter than about 10 picometres; the boundaries are not sharp

slides.narration: Here are the seven bands in order of rising frequency: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. A handy memory line is: Rich Men In Vegas Use eXpensive Gadgets. The ranges are approximate, and neighbouring bands blur into each other. X-rays and gamma rays even overlap: a wave of a given wavelength is called an X-ray if electrons made it and a gamma ray if a nucleus did.

slides.heading: The spectrum on a logarithmic scale
slides.body_md: Every band obeys $c = f\lambda$ in vacuum, so $f$ rises as $\lambda$ falls. On a logarithmic scale each step is a factor of 1000 in wavelength.
bullets: Visible light is a very narrow band, about 400–700 nm.
From ultraviolet upwards the radiation can **ionise** atoms and damage living cells.

slides.narration: The spectrum covers such a vast range that we draw it on a logarithmic scale, where each tick is a thousand times shorter in wavelength than the one before. Notice how tiny the visible band is, from about four hundred to seven hundred nanometres. Moving to the right, the frequency rises, and from ultraviolet onwards the radiation can knock electrons out of atoms, which is why it can harm living cells.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: which band?
slides.body_md: Use $c = f\lambda$ to name the band of (a) a wave of frequency 2.45 GHz, (b) radiation of wavelength 3.0 μm, (c) radiation of frequency $1.2 \times 10^{18}$ Hz.
bullets: (a) $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.45 \times 10^{9}} = 0.122$ m (12.2 cm): **microwave** (the frequency of a microwave oven).

visual.alt: Worked table: 2.45 gigahertz is 12.2 centimetres, a microwave; 3 micrometres is ten to the fourteen hertz, infrared; 1.2 times ten to the eighteen hertz is 0.25 nanometres, X-rays

slides.narration: Change whichever quantity is given into the other, then compare with the table. Two point four five gigahertz gives a wavelength of about twelve centimetres, a microwave: in fact the frequency used in microwave ovens. Three micrometres corresponds to ten to the fourteen hertz, in the infrared. And one point two times ten to the eighteen hertz has a wavelength of a quarter of a nanometre, an X-ray.

slides.heading: Radio waves
slides.body_md: Longest wavelengths, from about 30 cm to many kilometres.
bullets: Medium waves are reflected by the **ionosphere**, so they can reach beyond the horizon.

rows: Oscillating currents in transmitting aerials (electronic oscillators)
Receiving aerial with a tuned circuit (radio, TV sets)
AM and FM broadcasting, TV, two-way radio, radio astronomy (GMRT near Pune)

visual.alt: Table for radio waves: produced by oscillating currents in aerials, detected by an aerial and tuned circuit, used for broadcasting, television, two-way radio and radio astronomy

slides.narration: Radio waves are made by electrons surging back and forth in a transmitting aerial, driven by an electronic oscillator. A receiving aerial picks them up, and a tuned circuit selects one station. They carry AM and FM broadcasts and television, and radio telescopes such as the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune study the radio waves arriving from distant galaxies.

slides.heading: Microwaves
slides.body_md: About 1 mm to 30 cm (1 GHz to 300 GHz).
bullets: **Source:** magnetron (ovens), klystron, Gunn diodes and transistor oscillators (phones, Wi-Fi).
**Detection:** dish or horn aerial with a crystal (point-contact) diode.
**Uses:** radar, microwave ovens, mobile phones, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, satellite and DTH television links.

visual.alt: Wavelength against frequency for microwaves between half a gigahertz and six gigahertz: a falling curve, since the wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency; a phone band, a microwave oven and a Wi-Fi band are marked
visual.caption: Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength: λ (cm) = 30 ÷ f (GHz).

slides.narration: Microwaves come from special valves called magnetrons and klystrons, or from small semiconductor oscillators in phones and routers. Dishes and horns collect them, and a crystal diode detects them. Their short wavelengths make narrow beams for radar and satellite links, and water molecules in food absorb them strongly, which is how a microwave oven heats. On the graph, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: radar ranging
slides.body_md: An airport radar working at 3.0 GHz sends out a short pulse, and the echo from an aircraft returns 0.30 ms later. Find (a) the wavelength used, (b) the distance of the aircraft.
bullets: (a) $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{3.0 \times 10^{9}} = 0.10$ m (10 cm, a microwave).
(b) The pulse travels there and back: $d = \dfrac{ct}{2} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 0.30 \times 10^{-3}}{2} = 4.5 \times 10^{4}$ m (45 km).

nodes.label: Dish sends a short microwave pulse

visual.alt: Flow of radar ranging: a dish sends a short microwave pulse, it reflects from an aircraft, the echo returns after a time t, and the distance is the speed of light times t over two

slides.narration: At three gigahertz the wavelength is ten centimetres, well inside the microwave band. The pulse goes out to the aircraft and comes back, so in point three milliseconds it covers twice the distance. Light speed times time gives ninety kilometres for the round trip, so the aircraft is forty five kilometres away.

slides.heading: Infrared
slides.body_md: About 700 nm to 1 mm, just beyond red light.
bullets: Absorbed by water vapour and carbon dioxide: the basis of the greenhouse effect.

rows: Hot and warm bodies (Sun, heaters, human skin), infrared LEDs
Thermopile, bolometer, IR photodiodes and phototransistors, thermal cameras, skin (warmth)
Remote controls, non-contact thermometers, night vision, physiotherapy heat lamps, optical-fibre links, keeping greenhouses warm

visual.alt: Table for infrared: produced by hot and warm bodies and infrared LEDs, detected by thermopiles, bolometers, photodiodes, thermal cameras and the skin, used in remote controls, thermometers, night vision, heat therapy and fibre links

slides.narration: Every warm object gives out infrared, from the Sun and a room heater down to your own skin. We feel strong infrared as warmth. Instruments detect it with thermopiles and bolometers, which warm up, or with infrared photodiodes. It is used in remote controls, forehead thermometers, night-vision and thermal cameras, physiotherapy lamps, and the optical fibres that carry the internet.

slides.heading: Visible light
slides.body_md: About 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red): the only band our eyes detect.
bullets: **Source:** the Sun, flames, filament lamps, LEDs, lasers. **Detection:** the eye, photocells, camera sensors, photographic film.
**Uses:** seeing, photography, photosynthesis, optical communication.

visual.alt: Table of approximate wavelengths of the colours of visible light, from violet at 400 to 450 nanometres to red at 620 to 700 nanometres

slides.narration: Visible light is a sliver of the spectrum, from violet at about four hundred nanometres to red at about seven hundred. It comes from the Sun, flames, lamps, LEDs and lasers, and it is detected by the retina of the eye, by photocells and by the sensors in a camera. Plants use it for photosynthesis, and we use it to see.

slides.heading: Ultraviolet
slides.body_md: About 1 nm to 400 nm, just beyond violet.
bullets: **Source:** the Sun, mercury-vapour lamps, electric arcs (welding), UV LEDs. **Detection:** photocells, fluorescent materials, photographic film.
**Uses:** sterilising water and surfaces, checking banknotes (fluorescent marks), making vitamin D in the skin.
**Ozone** high in the atmosphere absorbs most solar UV; too much UV causes sunburn, eye damage and skin cancer.

slides.heading: X-rays
slides.body_md: About 1 pm to 1 nm.
bullets: They pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and metal; they ionise, so exposure is kept short and staff are shielded with lead.

rows: X-ray tube: fast electrons, accelerated through tens of kilovolts, strike a metal target such as tungsten
Photographic film, fluorescent screens, digital detectors, Geiger–Müller counters
Radiography of bones and teeth, CT scans, airport baggage checks, finding the arrangement of atoms in crystals

visual.alt: Table for X-rays: produced when fast electrons strike a metal target in an X-ray tube, detected by film, fluorescent screens, digital detectors and Geiger counters, used for radiography, CT scans, baggage checks and crystal studies

slides.narration: X-rays are made in an X-ray tube, where electrons accelerated through tens of thousands of volts slam into a metal target. They pass easily through flesh, cloth and plastic but are absorbed by bone and metal, so they cast shadow pictures on film or a digital detector. Their wavelengths are close to the spacing of atoms, so they also reveal how atoms are arranged in crystals. Because they ionise, staff shelter behind lead.

slides.heading: Gamma rays
slides.body_md: Shortest wavelengths, below about 10 pm: the most penetrating radiation.
bullets: They come from changes inside the **nucleus**, not from electrons; thick lead or concrete is needed to stop them.

rows: Radioactive nuclei (for example cobalt-60), nuclear reactions
Geiger–Müller counter, scintillation counter, photographic film
Radiotherapy for cancer, sterilising syringes and surgical gloves, food irradiation, checking welds in pipelines

slides.narration: Gamma rays come from inside the nucleus, when a radioactive nucleus such as cobalt sixty settles into a lower-energy state. Geiger counters and scintillation counters detect them. They are so penetrating and so damaging to cells that they are used to destroy tumours, to sterilise sealed packs of syringes and gloves, to stop stored onions and potatoes from sprouting, and to check thick metal welds for cracks.

sections.heading: 1. Displacement current
sections.body_md:
- **The problem:** Ampère’s law $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 i$ allows any surface bounded by the loop. For a loop round the lead of a charging capacitor, a flat disc encloses the current $i$, but a surface bulging through the gap encloses no conduction current: two answers for one loop.
- **Maxwell’s fix:** a changing electric flux acts as a current, the **displacement current** $i_d = \varepsilon_0\,\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$. Ampère–Maxwell law: $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0(i + i_d)$.
- For a parallel-plate capacitor: $\Phi_E = EA = q/\varepsilon_0$, so $i_d = dq/dt = i$: the current is **continuous** through the gap. Also $i_d = C\,dV/dt = \varepsilon_0A\,dE/dt$.
- The displacement current produces a magnetic field (circles round the axis of the plates) exactly like a conduction current. It exists only while E changes: zero once the capacitor is fully charged, so steady DC is blocked.
- Conduction current: moving charges in a conductor. Displacement current: changing E, possible even in vacuum. ISC: basic idea and formula only.

key_terms.definition_md: ε₀ dΦE/dt: the current-like effect of a changing electric flux, which produces a magnetic field.
Conduction current in the leads plus displacement current in the gap form one unbroken current round a circuit with a capacitor.

sections.heading: 2. Nature of electromagnetic waves
sections.body_md:
- A changing B produces E (Faraday); a changing E produces B (Maxwell). Each regenerates the other, so the disturbance travels through empty space.
- **Source:** accelerated charges, for example charges oscillating in an aerial; the wave has the frequency of the oscillation. A charge at rest or in uniform motion does not radiate.
- **Transverse:** in a plane wave along x, E oscillates along y and B along z: $\vec E \perp \vec B$, both perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is the direction of $\vec E \times \vec B$. E and B are **in phase**.
- Sketch: a sine curve of E in one plane and of B in the perpendicular plane, both on the same axis of travel, peaking together; label E, B, the direction of travel and λ.

key_terms.definition_md: Linked oscillating electric and magnetic fields, at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, moving at c in vacuum.
A wave whose oscillations are at right angles to its direction of travel.

sections.heading: 3. Speed and properties of EM waves
sections.body_md:
- Speed in vacuum: $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹. It matched the measured speed of light, so light is an EM wave; Hertz produced and detected radio waves to confirm the theory.
- Peak fields: $\dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = c$. For every EM wave in vacuum: $c = f\lambda$. In a material medium the speed is less than c (qualitative only).
- **Common properties:** transverse; same speed c in vacuum; no medium needed; E and B in phase; carry energy and momentum; uncharged, so not deflected by electric or magnetic fields; show reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarisation.
- The bands differ only in frequency (and so wavelength).

key_terms.definition_md: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the same for every EM wave.

sections.heading: 4. The electromagnetic spectrum: order and ranges
sections.body_md:
- Increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength): **radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays**.
- Approximate wavelengths: radio longer than 30 cm; microwaves 1 mm to 30 cm (1–300 GHz); infrared 700 nm to 1 mm; visible 400–700 nm; ultraviolet 1–400 nm; X-rays 1 pm to 1 nm; gamma rays below about 10 pm. Boundaries are not sharp.
- X-rays and gamma rays overlap; they are named by origin (electrons hitting a target, or nuclei).
- Place a wave in its band by converting with $c = f\lambda$. From ultraviolet upwards the radiation is **ionising**.

key_terms.definition_md: The whole range of EM waves arranged by frequency or wavelength, from radio waves to gamma rays.
Radiation able to knock electrons out of atoms: ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

sections.heading: 5. Radio waves, microwaves and infrared
sections.body_md:
- **Radio:** source — oscillating currents in aerials; detection — aerial with a tuned circuit; uses — AM and FM broadcasting, TV, two-way radio, radio astronomy. Medium waves are reflected by the ionosphere.
- **Microwaves:** source — magnetron, klystron, Gunn diode and transistor oscillators; detection — dish or horn with a crystal diode; uses — radar (distance = ct/2), microwave ovens (2.45 GHz, absorbed by water in food), mobile phones, Wi-Fi, satellite links (they pass through the ionosphere).
- **Infrared:** source — hot and warm bodies, IR LEDs; detection — thermopile, bolometer, IR photodiode, thermal camera, the skin; uses — remote controls, non-contact thermometers, night vision, physiotherapy, optical fibres, greenhouses (absorbed by water vapour and CO₂).

sections.heading: 6. Visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays
sections.body_md:
- **Visible (400–700 nm):** source — Sun, flames, lamps, LEDs, lasers; detection — eye, photocell, camera sensor, film; uses — vision, photography, photosynthesis.
- **Ultraviolet:** source — Sun, mercury-vapour lamps, welding arcs; detection — photocells, fluorescent materials, film; uses — sterilising water and surfaces, detecting forged notes, vitamin D. Mostly absorbed by the **ozone layer**; excess causes sunburn, eye damage, skin cancer.
- **X-rays:** source — fast electrons striking a metal target in an X-ray tube; detection — film, fluorescent screen, digital detector, GM counter; uses — radiography, CT scans, baggage checks, crystal structure (wavelengths near atomic spacing). Ionising: limit exposure, shield with lead.
- **Gamma rays:** source — radioactive nuclei (e.g. cobalt-60); detection — GM and scintillation counters; uses — radiotherapy, sterilising medical items, food irradiation, checking welds. Most penetrating.

key_terms.definition_md: Absorbing ultraviolet and giving out visible light; used to detect UV and to check banknotes.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Continuity of current: one loop, two surfaces; the gap surface needs the displacement current $\varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt$.
- For a capacitor, $i_d = C\,dV/dt$; it is zero once the capacitor is fully charged.
- Sketch E, B and the direction of travel mutually perpendicular, E and B in phase; $E_0 = cB_0$, $c = f\lambda$.
- Spectrum: order both ways, approximate ranges, and one source, detector and use for each band.

cards.front_md: Displacement current in terms of electric flux?
cards.back_md: $i_d = \varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt$.

cards.front_md: Why was displacement current needed?
cards.back_md: For a loop round a charging capacitor’s lead, a surface through the gap encloses no conduction current, so Ampère’s law gave two answers.

cards.front_md: Ampère–Maxwell law?
cards.back_md: $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0(i + i_d)$.

cards.front_md: Displacement current in a capacitor compared with the current in its leads?
cards.back_md: Equal: $i_d = dq/dt = i$, so the current is continuous.

cards.front_md: Displacement current from the p.d. across a capacitor?
cards.back_md: $i_d = C\,dV/dt$.

cards.front_md: Displacement current once a capacitor is fully charged?
cards.back_md: Zero: the electric field no longer changes.

cards.front_md: Shape of the magnetic field lines round a charging capacitor’s gap?
cards.back_md: Circles centred on the axis of the plates.

cards.front_md: What produces electromagnetic waves?
cards.back_md: Accelerated charges, such as charges oscillating in an aerial.

cards.front_md: Directions of E and B in an EM wave?
cards.back_md: Perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel ($\vec E \times \vec B$).

cards.front_md: Phase relation of E and B in a travelling EM wave?
cards.back_md: In phase: they peak together.

cards.front_md: Speed of EM waves in vacuum from μ₀ and ε₀?
cards.back_md: $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Ratio of the peak fields of an EM wave in vacuum?
Who first generated and detected radio waves in a laboratory?
cards.back_md: Heinrich Hertz (1887–88).

cards.front_md: Four properties shared by all EM waves?
cards.back_md: Transverse; speed c in vacuum; need no medium; carry energy and momentum (also uncharged, E and B in phase).

cards.front_md: E₀ = 90 V m⁻¹: B₀?
The spectrum in order of increasing frequency?
cards.back_md: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

cards.front_md: Wavelength range of visible light?

cards.front_md: Wavelength of a 6.0 GHz signal?

cards.back_md: Magnetron.

Two detectors of infrared?

cards.front_md: Two uses of infrared?

cards.front_md: What absorbs most of the Sun’s short-wave ultraviolet?

questions.stem_md: A circular loop is drawn round one lead of a capacitor while it charges with current i. A flat disc bounded by the loop is pierced by the lead. A second surface, bounded by the same loop, bulges out like a bag and passes between the plates. The conduction current crossing the bag-shaped surface is

options.text_md: i, exactly as for the flat disc
zero, so Ampère’s original law gives a different answer for each surface
2i, since the current both enters and leaves the bag
i/2, since the bag has twice the area of the disc

questions.solution_md: No charge crosses the gap between the plates, so the bag-shaped surface encloses no conduction current, while the flat disc encloses i. The same loop would have two different values of ∮B · dl, which is why Maxwell added the displacement current ε₀ dΦE/dt through the gap — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The p.d. across a 50 nF capacitor in a timing circuit rises steadily from 0 to 12 V in 3.0 ms. While it rises, the displacement current between the plates is

options.text_md: 2.0 mA

questions.solution_md: $i_d = C\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 50 \times 10^{-9} \times \dfrac{12}{3.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ A, i.e. 0.20 mA. 0.60 μC is the final charge (forgetting to divide by the time) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Viewed along the axis of a pair of circular plates while the capacitor they form is being charged, the magnetic field lines in and around the gap

options.text_md: are straight lines parallel to the electric field between the plates
point radially outwards from the axis
are circles centred on the axis, as round a wire carrying the charging current
do not exist, because no charge crosses the gap

questions.solution_md: The displacement current through the gap produces a magnetic field exactly like a conduction current: closed circles round the axis, whose sense follows the right-hand rule — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? While a camera-flash capacitor discharges through the flash tube, a displacement current exists in the gap between its plates.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. As the plates lose charge the electric field in the gap falls, so the electric flux is changing and ε₀ dΦE/dt is not zero; it equals the discharge current, in the opposite sense to the charging case.

questions.stem_md: In Maxwell’s term ε₀ dΦE/dt the electric flux ΦE is in volt metres and ε₀ in C² N⁻¹ m⁻², so the product works out in ___, the unit of current.
questions.solution_md: C² N⁻¹ m⁻² × V m s⁻¹ = C² N⁻¹ m⁻¹ s⁻¹ × (N m C⁻¹) = C s⁻¹, i.e. **amperes**: the displacement current is a genuine current in its units and in its magnetic effect.

questions.stem_md: The 400 μF capacitor of a photographic flash unit charges with its p.d. rising at an average 250 V s⁻¹. Find the average displacement current between its plates, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: $i_d = C\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 400 \times 10^{-6} \times 250 = 0.10$ A, the same as the charging current in the leads.

questions.stem_md: A capacitor has square plates of side 12 cm. While it charges, the electric field in the gap grows by 1.5 × 10¹¹ V m⁻¹ every second. How large is the displacement current through the gap? Give your answer in mA to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = A\dfrac{dE}{dt} = (0.12)^2 \times 1.5 \times 10^{11} = 2.16 \times 10^{9}$ V m s$^{-1}$; $i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 2.16 \times 10^{9} = 0.0191$ A, i.e. $0.0191 \times 10^{3} = 19.1$ mA.

marking_scheme.step: dΦE/dt = A dE/dt = 2.16 × 10⁹ V m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: A displacement current of 5.0 mA is to be set up between the plates of a 2.5 nF capacitor. At what rate must the p.d. across it change? Answer in megavolts per second (MV s⁻¹).
At what rate must the electric flux through a surface change for a displacement current of 1.0 A to cross it? Give the answer in units of 10¹¹ V m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \dfrac{i_d}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{1.0}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = 1.13 \times 10^{11}$ V m s$^{-1}$, i.e. $\dfrac{1.13 \times 10^{11}}{10^{11}} = 1.13$ in units of $10^{11}$ V m s$^{-1}$: a very fast change for a modest current.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a capacitor is switched on to a battery through a resistor, the displacement current between its plates is largest at the very first instant.

**Reason (R):** The displacement current is proportional to the rate of change of the electric flux between the plates.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: i_d = ε₀ dΦE/dt equals the charging current, which is largest at switch-on when the uncharged capacitor offers no opposing p.d.; the field then grows fastest, and its growth slows as the plates fill — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A steady direct current can keep flowing indefinitely round a circuit that contains a capacitor in series.

**Reason (R):** A displacement current exists in the gap of a capacitor only while the electric field there is changing.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: once the capacitor is fully charged the field in the gap stops changing, the displacement current falls to zero, and with no current across the gap the current in the rest of the series circuit stops too — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A capacitor is being charged from a battery. Charge flows in the wires but never across the gap between the plates. Explain how the idea of displacement current makes the current continuous round this circuit.

answer.model_answer_md: In the gap no charge moves, but the electric field, and so the electric flux, is **changing** as charge builds up. This acts as a **displacement current** ε₀ dΦE/dt, which equals the conduction current i in the wires. So conduction current in the leads and displacement current in the gap form one **continuous** current, with the same magnetic effect everywhere.

questions.solution_md: Changing flux in the gap gives i_d = i.

marking_scheme.step: Changing electric flux in the gap acts as a displacement current
It equals the conduction current, so the current is continuous

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between the conduction current in the copper leads of a charging capacitor and the displacement current in its gap, and one way in which they are alike.

answer.model_answer_md: Differences: (i) conduction current is the drift of **charges** through a conductor, while displacement current is a **changing electric field** with no charge moving; (ii) conduction current needs a conductor, while displacement current can exist in an insulator or even **vacuum**. Alike: both produce a **magnetic field** in exactly the same way.

questions.solution_md: Moving charge versus changing E; conductor versus anywhere; both make B.

questions.stem_md: A parallel-plate capacitor with plates of area A is being charged; at some instant the charge on its positive plate is q. Starting from E = q/(ε₀A) for the field in the gap, prove that ε₀ dΦE/dt across the gap equals the current in the connecting wires, and state what this result means for Ampère’s circuital law.

answer.model_answer_md:
The field between the plates is uniform: $E = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0A}$, so the electric flux through the gap is $\Phi_E = EA = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$.
Then $i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \varepsilon_0 \cdot \dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{dq}{dt} = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = i$, the current in the wires.
Meaning: if the displacement current is added to the conduction current, $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0(i + i_d)$, every surface bounded by a loop round the lead gives the same total current $i$, so the Ampère–Maxwell law is consistent.

questions.solution_md: ΦE = q/ε₀, so ε₀ dΦE/dt = dq/dt.

marking_scheme.step: Ampère–Maxwell law gives the same answer for every surface

questions.stem_md: The charge on the positive plate of a capacitor rises steadily from zero to 10 μC between t = 0 and t = 2.5 ms, stays at 10 μC until t = 6.0 ms, and then falls steadily to zero by t = 7.0 ms. Find the displacement current between the plates in each of the three intervals, and compare its direction in the first and last.

answer.model_answer_md:
For a parallel-plate capacitor $i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \dfrac{dq}{dt}$, the slope of the $q$–$t$ graph.
0 to 2.5 ms: $i_d = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ A (4.0 mA).
2.5 ms to 6.0 ms: the charge, and so the field, is constant: $i_d = 0$.
6.0 ms to 7.0 ms: $|i_d| = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.010$ A (10 mA), two and a half times as large and in the **opposite** direction, since the field is now falling.

questions.solution_md: i_d = slope of q against t.

marking_scheme.step: Zero while the charge is steady

questions.stem_md: The plates of an air-filled capacitor each have an area of 0.25 m² and are 2.0 mm apart. The p.d. between them is increasing at 5.0 × 10⁴ V s⁻¹. Find (a) the capacitance, (b) the rate at which the electric field in the gap grows, (c) the displacement current, and compare it with the current in the leads.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d} = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.25}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.11 \times 10^{-9}$ F (about 1.1 nF).
(b) $E = \dfrac{V}{d}$, so $\dfrac{dE}{dt} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{4}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.5 \times 10^{7}$ V m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.
(c) $i_d = \varepsilon_0A\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.25 \times 2.5 \times 10^{7} = 5.53 \times 10^{-5}$ A (55.3 μA). The lead current is $C\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 1.11 \times 10^{-9} \times 5.0 \times 10^{4} = 5.53 \times 10^{-5}$ A: the same.

questions.solution_md: C = ε₀A/d; dE/dt = (dV/dt)/d; i_d = ε₀A dE/dt = C dV/dt.

marking_scheme.step: i_d ≈ 5.53 × 10⁻⁵ A, equal to the lead current

questions.stem_md: A weather balloon carries a receiver straight above a ground transmitter, so the radio waves reaching it travel vertically upwards. At the balloon, the electric and magnetic fields of the wave oscillate

options.text_md: both vertically, along the direction of travel
both in horizontal directions, at right angles to each other
E vertically and B horizontally
both horizontally, parallel to each other

questions.solution_md: EM waves are transverse: E and B are both perpendicular to the direction of travel (here vertical), so both lie in the horizontal plane, and they are also perpendicular to each other — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A radio wave travels due north over flat ground. At one instant, at a certain point, its electric field points due east. At that point and instant its magnetic field points

options.text_md: vertically upwards
due west
vertically downwards
due south

questions.solution_md: The direction of travel is that of $\vec E \times \vec B$. With x east, y north, z up: $\hat x \times (-\hat z) = +\hat y$ (north), so $\vec B$ points vertically **downwards**. Upwards would send the wave south; B cannot be along E (west is antiparallel to E) or along the direction of travel — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For any electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum, the peak electric field divided by the peak magnetic field, E₀/B₀, equals

options.text_md: 1, since the electric and magnetic parts carry equal energy
the speed of light, 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
μ₀ε₀
the frequency of the wave

questions.solution_md: E₀ = cB₀ for every EM wave in vacuum, so E₀/B₀ = c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ (V m⁻¹ divided by T gives m s⁻¹) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A lightning stroke 3 km away produces a flash of light, a crackle of radio interference on an AM radio, and thunder. Which arrive at the same moment?

options.text_md: The flash and the radio crackle, both electromagnetic waves travelling at c
The radio crackle and the thunder, both of low frequency
All three, since they start together
None: the radio crackle arrives last because its wavelength is longest

questions.solution_md: Light and radio waves are both EM waves and travel at the same speed c in air (very nearly), taking about 10 μs for 3 km; sound takes about 9 s — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Imagine a universe in which the permittivity of free space ε₀ were four times its actual value, with μ₀ unchanged. Light in vacuum would travel

options.text_md: at half its actual speed
at twice its actual speed
at a quarter of its actual speed
at the same speed, since c is a universal constant

questions.solution_md: $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}}$, so four times $\varepsilon_0$ gives $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt 4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ of the speed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Using μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², calculate the speed 1/√(μ₀ε₀) that Maxwell’s theory predicts for electromagnetic waves, in units of 10⁸ m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
A few metres from a home Wi-Fi router, the peak electric field of its signal is 0.60 V m⁻¹. Find the peak magnetic field of the signal there, in nanotesla.
questions.solution_md: $B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c} = \dfrac{0.60}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-9}$ T, i.e. $2.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 10^{9} = 2.0$ nT, about ten thousand times weaker than the Earth’s field.

questions.stem_md: Close to the dish of a ship’s radar, the peak magnetic field of the microwave beam is 4.5 μT. Find the peak electric field of the beam, in kV m⁻¹.
A ground station in Karnataka sends a radio command to a spacecraft orbiting near the Moon, 3.84 × 10⁸ m away. How long does the command take to arrive, in seconds (3 significant figures)?
questions.solution_md: Radio waves travel at $c$ through the near-vacuum of space: $t = \dfrac{d}{c} = \dfrac{3.84 \times 10^{8}}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 1.28$ s.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Sunlight reaches the Earth across about 150 million km of almost empty space because electromagnetic waves, unlike sound, need no material medium to travel through.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. An EM wave consists of electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each other; they need no particles to vibrate, so the wave crosses vacuum at c.

questions.stem_md: Maxwell predicted that changing fields would travel at 1/√(μ₀ε₀); the German physicist ___ confirmed it in 1887–88 by producing radio waves with a spark gap and detecting them across his laboratory.
questions.solution_md: **Heinrich Hertz** generated radio waves with an oscillating spark circuit, detected them with a loop and gap, and showed that they could be reflected, refracted and polarised like light.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At a point where the electric field of a travelling electromagnetic wave in vacuum is momentarily zero, its magnetic field is also zero.

**Reason (R):** In a travelling EM wave in vacuum, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate in phase, with E = cB at every instant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: since E = cB at every point and instant, E and B pass through zero together and reach their peaks together — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An electron moving in a circle at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field radiates electromagnetic waves.

**Reason (R):** A charge radiates only when the magnitude of its velocity changes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the electron’s velocity keeps changing direction, so it has a centripetal acceleration, and any accelerated charge radiates. R is false: a change of direction alone is an acceleration and is enough — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Radio waves from a cricket commentary and gamma rays from a hospital’s cobalt unit seem to have nothing in common. Name four properties that they nevertheless share as electromagnetic waves.

answer.model_answer_md: Both (i) are **transverse**, with E and B perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel; (ii) travel at the same speed **c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹** in vacuum; (iii) need **no medium**; (iv) carry **energy and momentum**, and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields. They differ only in frequency.

questions.solution_md: Transverse; speed c; no medium; energy and momentum.

questions.stem_md: Show that 1/√(μ₀ε₀) works out to about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and state the conclusion Maxwell drew from this value.

answer.model_answer_md: Multiplying the two constants, $\mu_0\varepsilon_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \approx 1.11 \times 10^{-17}$ s² m⁻², whose square root is about $3.34 \times 10^{-9}$ s m⁻¹, so $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} \approx 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹. This equals the measured **speed of light**, although both constants come from experiments on charges and currents, so Maxwell concluded that **light is an electromagnetic wave**.

questions.solution_md: c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the speed of light.

questions.stem_md: A plane electromagnetic wave travels along the +z axis, and its electric field oscillates along the x axis. Sketch (describe in words) the wave over one wavelength, labelling E, B and the direction of travel; state the axis along which B oscillates; and find the peak magnetic field if the peak electric field is 15 V m⁻¹.

answer.model_answer_md:
Sketch: along the z axis, a sine curve of $\vec E$ drawn in the x–z plane and a sine curve of $\vec B$ drawn in the y–z plane, with the same wavelength λ marked, both crossing zero and peaking at the same points (in phase); an arrow along +z labelled “direction of travel”.
$\vec B$ oscillates along the **y axis**, since the direction of travel is that of $\vec E \times \vec B$ and $\hat x \times \hat y = \hat z$.
$B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c} = \dfrac{15}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-8}$ T.

questions.solution_md: E along x, travel along z, so B along y; B₀ = E₀/c.

marking_scheme.step: Sketch: E and B perpendicular sine curves, in phase, on the axis of travel
B along y (from E × B along +z)

questions.stem_md: Explain how the laws of Faraday and Maxwell together allow an electromagnetic disturbance to travel through empty space, and why charges oscillating in a transmitting aerial send out such waves while a steady current in the same aerial does not.

answer.model_answer_md: By **Faraday’s law** a changing magnetic field produces an electric field; by **Maxwell’s** displacement-current idea a changing electric field produces a magnetic field. So once the fields start changing, each change regenerates the other and the linked pattern moves outward at c, needing no medium. Charges oscillating in an aerial are **accelerated**, so the fields round them keep changing and radiate as waves of the oscillation frequency. A steady current has unchanging fields, and charges in uniform motion do not radiate.

questions.solution_md: Changing B makes E; changing E makes B; accelerated charges start it.

marking_scheme.step: Changing E produces B (Maxwell): mutual regeneration travels at c
Accelerated charges radiate; steady current gives no changing fields

questions.stem_md: A hospital uses radio waves in its MRI scanner, infrared in a physiotherapy heat lamp, ultraviolet in an operating-theatre steriliser and X-rays in its radiography room. Arranged in order of increasing wavelength, these are

options.text_md: radio waves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays
X-rays, infrared, ultraviolet, radio waves
X-rays, ultraviolet, infrared, radio waves
ultraviolet, X-rays, radio waves, infrared

questions.solution_md: Wavelength increases from X-rays (about 1 pm to 1 nm) through ultraviolet (1–400 nm) and infrared (700 nm to 1 mm) to radio waves (longer than 30 cm) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The remote key of a car sends its unlock code at 433 MHz. The wavelength of this signal, and its band, are

options.text_md: about 6.9 cm, microwaves
about 6.9 m, radio waves (short wave)
about 0.69 mm, infrared
about 69 cm, radio waves (UHF)

questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{433 \times 10^{6}} = 0.69$ m, about 69 cm: longer than 30 cm, so radio waves in the UHF range — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Airport security scanners pass X-rays through suitcases to form an image of their contents. X-rays suit this job because they

options.text_md: are reflected strongly by cloth and plastic
pass through cloth, leather and plastic but are absorbed much more by dense metal objects
make metal objects give out visible light of their own
bend round metal objects and so outline them

questions.solution_md: X-rays penetrate light, low-density materials easily but are strongly absorbed by dense materials such as metal, which therefore cast clear shadows on the detector — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Sealed packs of surgical gloves are sterilised by gamma rays. These rays are emitted by

options.text_md: fast electrons striking a tungsten target
a magnetron
radioactive nuclei, such as those of cobalt-60
a mercury-vapour lamp

questions.solution_md: Gamma rays come from changes inside the nucleus, as when a radioactive cobalt-60 nucleus settles to a lower-energy state. Electrons hitting a target give X-rays, a magnetron gives microwaves, and a mercury lamp gives ultraviolet — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A shopkeeper slides a ₹500 note under a small lamp in a dark box; hidden fibres and marks on a genuine note glow brightly. The lamp mainly emits

options.text_md: ultraviolet radiation
infrared radiation
microwaves
gamma rays

questions.solution_md: Security inks and fibres fluoresce: they absorb ultraviolet and give out visible light, so they glow under a UV lamp while forged paper usually does not — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Scientists use X-rays, rather than visible light, to work out how atoms are arranged inside a crystal of common salt. The main reason is that X-ray wavelengths are

options.text_md: far longer than the spacing of atoms, so they pass through without scattering
the same as those of gamma rays, which nuclei emit
able to travel faster than light inside the crystal
comparable to the spacing of atoms (about 0.1 nm), so the atomic layers diffract them

questions.solution_md: Diffraction is strong when the wavelength is similar to the spacing of the obstacles. Atoms in a crystal are about 0.1–0.3 nm apart, like X-ray wavelengths, while visible light (400–700 nm) is thousands of times too long — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A nurse checks a child’s temperature with a thermometer gun held a few centimetres from the forehead, without touching it. The gun works by

options.text_md: detecting the infrared radiation given out by the warm skin
sending out ultraviolet and measuring the reflection
detecting microwaves given out by the blood
measuring the visible light reflected by the skin

questions.solution_md: Every warm body emits infrared; the gun focuses the skin’s infrared onto a thermopile or similar sensor, and more radiation means a higher temperature — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Gamma rays from a cobalt-60 source travel faster through a vacuum than the visible light from a candle flame, because gamma rays have a much higher frequency.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum; a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, not a higher speed.

questions.stem_md: The vacuum valve that generates the 2.45 GHz waves inside a kitchen microwave oven is called a ___.
questions.solution_md: A **magnetron**: electrons circling in a magnetic field past resonant cavities produce intense microwaves.

questions.stem_md: Match each radiation in Column A with a device in Column B that is used to detect it.

options.text_md: Radio waves
Infrared
Ultraviolet
Gamma rays

match_right.text_md: A thermopile or bolometer that warms up when the radiation falls on it
An aerial joined to a tuned LC circuit
A screen coated with a fluorescent material that glows

questions.solution_md: Radio → aerial and tuned circuit (1 → r); infrared → thermopile or bolometer (2 → p); ultraviolet → fluorescent screen (3 → s); gamma rays → Geiger–Müller counter (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Match each job in Column A, seen in an Indian city, with the radiation in Column B that does it.

options.text_md: A traffic police radar gun measures a car’s speed
A municipal plant disinfects drinking water
A dental clinic photographs a hidden tooth root
An internet provider carries data along glass fibres

questions.solution_md: Speed gun → microwaves (radar) (1 → s); water disinfection → ultraviolet (2 → q); dental image → X-rays (3 → p); fibre link → infrared, near 1550 nm (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: A thermal camera at an airport arrival hall picks up radiation from travellers’ skin, which is strongest near a wavelength of 9.5 μm. Find the frequency of this radiation, in terahertz (1 THz = 10¹² Hz), to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{9.5 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.16 \times 10^{13}$ Hz, i.e. $\dfrac{3.16 \times 10^{13}}{10^{12}} = 31.6$ THz, in the infrared.

questions.stem_md: A “black light” tube used to inspect banknotes emits ultraviolet of wavelength 365 nm. Find its frequency, in units of 10¹⁴ Hz (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{365 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.22 \times 10^{14}$ Hz, i.e. $\dfrac{8.22 \times 10^{14}}{10^{14}} = 8.22$ in units of $10^{14}$ Hz, just above the violet end of the visible band.

questions.stem_md: A dental X-ray unit produces radiation of frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Find its wavelength, in picometres (1 pm = 10⁻¹² m).
One of the observing bands of the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune is centred on 610 MHz. Find the wavelength at this frequency, in metres (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{610 \times 10^{6}} = 0.492$ m, about half a metre: radio waves, as the telescope’s name suggests.

questions.stem_md: A rooftop DTH dish receives television signals from a satellite at 12 GHz. Find their wavelength, in centimetres.
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{12 \times 10^{9}} = 0.025$ m, i.e. $0.025 \times 100 = 2.5$ cm: microwaves, which pass through the ionosphere to and from the satellite.

questions.stem_md: Long-distance optical fibres carry internet data on infrared of wavelength 1550 nm. Find the frequency of this radiation, in terahertz (3 significant figures).
A weather radar near Chennai sends out a microwave pulse, and the echo from a rain cloud returns 0.40 ms after the pulse leaves. How far away is the cloud, in kilometres?
questions.solution_md: The pulse goes out and back, so $d = \dfrac{ct}{2} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 0.40 \times 10^{-3}}{2} = 6.0 \times 10^{4}$ m, i.e. $\dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{4}}{10^{3}} = 60$ km.

questions.stem_md: A radio amateur talks to distant stations on the 40 m short-wave band, and links two buildings with a 2.4 GHz microwave link. Find the frequency of the 40 m band, and hence how many times higher the link frequency is.
questions.solution_md: $f_1 = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{40} = 7.5 \times 10^{6}$ Hz (7.5 MHz). $\dfrac{f_2}{f_1} = \dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{9}}{7.5 \times 10^{6}} = 320$ times higher.

questions.stem_md: A simple TV aerial is a half-wave dipole: two rods whose total length is half a wavelength. How long should it be for a UHF channel at 750 MHz? Answer in centimetres.
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{750 \times 10^{6}} = 0.40$ m, so the dipole is $\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 0.20$ m, i.e. $0.20 \times 100 = 20$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Almost none of the Sun’s short-wave ultraviolet (UV-C) reaches the ground.

**Reason (R):** UV-C has a shorter wavelength than visible light.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A: wavelength alone does not decide whether the atmosphere absorbs a radiation (it lets through visible light and also many far longer radio waves). UV-C is stopped because ozone and oxygen molecules high in the atmosphere absorb it strongly — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than infrared radiation.

**Reason (R):** Microwaves have lower frequencies than infrared radiation.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: microwaves (up to about 300 GHz) lie below infrared in frequency. A is false: since c = fλ is the same for both, the lower-frequency microwaves have the longer wavelengths (1 mm to 30 cm against 700 nm to 1 mm) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: When a button on a TV remote is pressed, the LED at its tip looks dark to the eye, but on a phone camera’s screen it is seen flashing. Explain both observations.

answer.model_answer_md: The LED emits **infrared**, of wavelength just beyond 700 nm, to which the retina is **not sensitive**, so the eye sees nothing. The silicon sensor in the phone camera **is** sensitive to near infrared, so it records the flashes and the screen shows them as visible light.

questions.solution_md: IR: invisible to the eye, detected by the camera sensor.

marking_scheme.step: Remote emits infrared, beyond the eye’s range
Camera sensor detects near infrared and displays it

questions.stem_md: A radiation of wavelength 0.010 nm can be called an X-ray or a gamma ray. Evaluate whether the two names describe different radiations, and say on what basis the name is given.

answer.model_answer_md: At the same wavelength they are **identical** EM waves with the same frequency and properties; the X-ray and gamma-ray bands **overlap**. The name depends on the **origin**: X-rays come from fast electrons striking a target (electron processes), gamma rays from changes inside atomic **nuclei**.

questions.solution_md: Same radiation; named by origin.

marking_scheme.step: Same wavelength means physically identical radiation; the bands overlap
Named by origin: electrons for X-rays, nuclei for gamma rays

questions.stem_md: In a microwave oven, a bowl of dal becomes hot while the dry ceramic plate under it stays fairly cool at first. Explain this, naming the band of radiation used.

answer.model_answer_md: The oven uses **microwaves** (2.45 GHz). They are absorbed strongly by **water** molecules in the dal, whose energy rises, so the food heats up. Dry ceramic contains little water and absorbs little microwave energy, so the plate warms mainly by **conduction** from the hot food.

questions.solution_md: Microwaves absorbed by water; dry ceramic absorbs little.

marking_scheme.step: Microwaves absorbed by water in the food
Dry ceramic absorbs little; warms only by conduction

questions.stem_md: During an epidemic, airports screened passengers with thermal cameras. Explain how such a camera forms its picture without any lamp, and why a passenger with a fever shows up differently.

answer.model_answer_md: All warm bodies **emit infrared**; the camera focuses this onto an array of infrared sensors and shows the intensity as colours, so no lamp is needed. A hotter body emits **more infrared**, so a feverish face appears brighter (a different colour) than those of other passengers.

questions.solution_md: Emitted IR; hotter emits more.

marking_scheme.step: Camera detects infrared emitted by the body itself
Hotter skin emits more infrared, so it appears brighter

questions.stem_md: Using c = fλ, name the band of each of these radiations, showing your working: (a) a wave of wavelength 3.0 mm from a car’s collision-warning radar, (b) radiation of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz from a sterilising lamp, (c) radiation of frequency 6.0 × 10¹³ Hz from a warm engine.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $f = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{3.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.0 \times 10^{11}$ Hz (100 GHz); 3.0 mm lies between 1 mm and 30 cm: **microwaves**.
(b) $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.5 \times 10^{15}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$ m (200 nm), shorter than 400 nm: **ultraviolet**.
(c) $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.0 \times 10^{13}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-6}$ m (5.0 μm), between 700 nm and 1 mm: **infrared**.

questions.solution_md: Convert with c = fλ and compare with the band ranges.

questions.stem_md: For each of (i) microwaves, (ii) infrared and (iii) ultraviolet, give the approximate wavelength range, one way of producing the radiation and one way of detecting it.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Microwaves:** about 1 mm to 30 cm; produced by a magnetron or klystron (or a Gunn diode); detected by a dish or horn with a crystal diode. (ii) **Infrared:** about 700 nm to 1 mm; produced by hot bodies or infrared LEDs; detected by a thermopile, bolometer or infrared photodiode. (iii) **Ultraviolet:** about 1 nm to 400 nm; produced by the Sun, mercury-vapour lamps or electric arcs; detected by photocells or fluorescent screens.

questions.solution_md: Range, source and detector for each.

questions.stem_md: Describe briefly how X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube. Explain why X-rays can show (i) a fractured bone in an arm, and (ii) the regular arrangement of atoms in a crystal, and why the radiographer stays behind a lead-lined wall.

answer.model_answer_md: In an evacuated tube, electrons from a hot filament are accelerated through tens of kilovolts and **strike a metal target** (such as tungsten); their sudden stopping produces X-rays. (i) X-rays pass easily through soft tissue but are **absorbed strongly by bone**, so the bone and its crack show as a shadow on the detector. (ii) Their wavelengths (about 0.1 nm) are **similar to the spacing of atoms**, so the atomic layers diffract them in a regular pattern. X-rays are **ionising**, so repeated exposure would harm the radiographer; lead absorbs them.

questions.solution_md: Fast electrons hit a target; absorption by bone; diffraction by atoms; ionising.

marking_scheme.step: Production: fast electrons striking a metal target
Bone absorbs more than tissue; wavelength near atomic spacing

questions.stem_md: A shop advertises a hand-held UV-C lamp “to disinfect your hands and face in seconds”. Evaluate this advertisement, explaining how ultraviolet kills germs and why sunlight at ground level contains almost no UV-C.

answer.model_answer_md: UV-C does **kill germs**: it is absorbed by their genetic material and damages it, which is why UV-C lamps sterilise water, air and empty rooms. But the same damage happens to **human skin and eyes**: UV-C can burn skin and cause painful eye injury, so shining it on hands and faces is **unsafe**, and the advertisement is misleading. It is suitable only for surfaces and water with people shielded. Sunlight at ground level has almost no UV-C because the **ozone layer** and oxygen high in the atmosphere absorb it.

questions.solution_md: Kills germs, but harms skin and eyes; ozone absorbs solar UV-C.

marking_scheme.step: UV-C damages the genetic material of germs
Also harms skin and eyes: unsafe on people, so the claim is misleading

questions.stem_md: (a) A loop is drawn round one lead of a capacitor that is being charged. Using two surfaces bounded by this loop, explain why Ampère’s circuital law, ∮B · dl = μ₀i, needed to be modified. [2] (b) Write the expression for the displacement current and the modified (Ampère–Maxwell) law. [1] (c) A capacitor with circular plates of radius 4.0 cm, 1.5 mm apart in air, is charged by a constant current of 0.15 A. Find (i) the rate at which the electric field between the plates increases, (ii) the rate at which the p.d. across the plates increases, (iii) the displacement current in the gap. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For a flat surface bounded by the loop, the lead pierces it and the enclosed current is $i$. For a bag-shaped surface on the same loop that passes between the plates, no charge crosses it, so the enclosed current is zero. Ampère’s law would give two different values of $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l$ for one loop, so it was incomplete for changing currents.

(b) $i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$; $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0(i + i_d)$.

(c) $A = \pi(0.040)^2 = 5.03 \times 10^{-3}$ m².
(i) $i = \varepsilon_0A\dfrac{dE}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{dE}{dt} = \dfrac{0.15}{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 5.03 \times 10^{-3}} = 3.37 \times 10^{12}$ V m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.
(ii) $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = d\,\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.37 \times 10^{12} = 5.06 \times 10^{9}$ V s$^{-1}$ (check: $C = \varepsilon_0A/d = 2.97 \times 10^{-11}$ F and $i/C$ gives the same).
(iii) $i_d = \varepsilon_0A\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 0.15$ A, equal to the charging current.

questions.stem_md: (a) An electromagnetic wave travels along the +y axis; at a certain point and instant its electric field points along +z. Draw (describe in words) a labelled sketch of the wave and state the direction of its magnetic field at that point and instant. [2] (b) Write the expression for the speed of EM waves in vacuum in terms of μ₀ and ε₀, and the relation between the peak fields. [1] (c) A green laser pointer emits light of wavelength 532 nm with a peak electric field of 600 V m⁻¹. Find the frequency, the period of oscillation and the peak magnetic field. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Sketch: along the y axis, a sine curve for $\vec E$ in the y–z plane and one for $\vec B$ in the x–y plane, with the same wavelength, peaking and crossing zero together (in phase); E, B, λ and the direction of travel (+y) labelled. Since the direction of travel is that of $\vec E \times \vec B$ and $\hat z \times \hat x = \hat y$, the magnetic field points along **+x**.

(b) $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹; $\dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = c$.

(c) $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{532 \times 10^{-9}} = 5.64 \times 10^{14}$ Hz; $T = \dfrac{1}{f} = 1.77 \times 10^{-15}$ s; $B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c} = \dfrac{600}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}$ T.

questions.solution_md: E × B along the travel; c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀); f = c/λ; B₀ = E₀/c.

marking_scheme.step: Sketch: perpendicular E and B curves, in phase, on the axis of travel

questions.stem_md: A smartphone handles several kinds of electromagnetic wave: an FM radio station at 98.3 MHz, a Wi-Fi network at 5.0 GHz, an infrared proximity sensor working at 850 nm, and visible light through its camera. (a) Find the wavelengths of the FM and Wi-Fi signals and the frequency of the infrared. [2] (b) Name the band of each of the four and arrange them in order of increasing frequency. [1] (c) Name a detector used for infrared and one for visible light. [1] (d) Why does the phone’s camera show the infrared sensor glowing when the eye sees nothing? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) FM: $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{98.3 \times 10^{6}} = 3.05$ m. Wi-Fi: $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{5.0 \times 10^{9}} = 0.060$ m (6.0 cm). Infrared: $f = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{850 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.53 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

(b) FM: radio waves; Wi-Fi: microwaves; 850 nm: infrared; camera: visible. Increasing frequency: FM radio, Wi-Fi microwaves, infrared, visible light.

(c) Infrared: a photodiode (or thermopile); visible light: the camera’s image sensor (or the eye, a photocell).

(d) The silicon camera sensor responds to near infrared just beyond 700 nm, but the retina does not, so the sensor records the 850 nm light and the screen displays it as visible light.

questions.solution_md: c = fλ for each; order radio, microwave, IR, visible.

marking_scheme.step: FM λ ≈ 3.05 m; Wi-Fi λ = 0.060 m
Camera sensor responds to near IR; eye does not

questions.stem_md: An airport surveillance radar works at 5.6 GHz. (a) Give two reasons why microwaves, rather than medium-wave radio, are used for radar. [1] (b) Find the wavelength of the radar waves. [1] (c) The echo from an approaching aircraft returns 120 μs after a pulse is sent; 10 s later the echo time is 100 μs. Find the two distances and the average speed of the aircraft towards the radar. [2] (d) At the aircraft, the peak electric field of the radar wave is 1.5 V m⁻¹. Find the peak magnetic field there. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Microwaves have short wavelengths, so a dish of modest size forms a **narrow beam** that can locate targets precisely, and small objects reflect them well; they also pass through cloud and through the ionosphere rather than being reflected by it.

(b) $\lambda = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{5.6 \times 10^{9}} = 0.0536$ m (about 5.4 cm).

(c) $d = \dfrac{ct}{2}$: $d_1 = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 120 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 1.8 \times 10^{4}$ m (18 km); $d_2 = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 100 \times 10^{-6}}{2} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}$ m (15 km). Speed $= \dfrac{18\,000 - 15\,000}{10} = 300$ m s$^{-1}$.

(d) $B_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{c} = \dfrac{1.5}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-9}$ T.

questions.solution_md: Narrow beams; λ = c/f; d = ct/2; B₀ = E₀/c.

marking_scheme.step: Short wavelength: narrow beam, good reflection (and passes cloud)
18 km and 15 km from d = ct/2

questions.stem_md: Infrared and ultraviolet lie on either side of the visible band. (a) Give one source and one detector of each. [2] (b) A non-contact thermometer gun is pointed at a patient’s forehead. Which of the two radiations does it use, and why does its reading depend on skin temperature? [1] (c) Hidden marks on a banknote glow under a “black light”. Name the radiation and explain the glow. [1] (d) Find the frequencies of ultraviolet of wavelength 380 nm and infrared of wavelength 10 μm, and the ratio of the first to the second. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Infrared: source, any hot or warm body (heater, the Sun, an IR LED); detector, a thermopile, bolometer or IR photodiode. Ultraviolet: source, the Sun, a mercury-vapour lamp or a welding arc; detector, a photocell or a fluorescent screen.

(b) Infrared: every warm body emits infrared, and a hotter body emits more of it, so the sensor’s signal rises with skin temperature.

(c) Ultraviolet: the security ink is fluorescent, absorbing the invisible ultraviolet and re-emitting visible light, so the marks glow.

(d) $f_{UV} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{380 \times 10^{-9}} = 7.89 \times 10^{14}$ Hz; $f_{IR} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{10 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.0 \times 10^{13}$ Hz; ratio $= \dfrac{7.89 \times 10^{14}}{3.0 \times 10^{13}} \approx 26.3$.

questions.solution_md: Sources and detectors; IR thermometry; UV fluorescence; f = c/λ.

marking_scheme.step: Thermometer: infrared, more emitted when hotter
Banknote: UV absorbed, visible light emitted (fluorescence)
